The Smoothing-Parameter Correction to the Effective Degrees of Freedom

Source: R/outer_hessian.R
statmod_edf_correction.Rd

Returns the amount by which \(\mathrm{tr}[(H+S)^{-1}H]\) understates the complexity of a fit whose hyperparameters were themselves estimated.

Usage

statmod_edf_correction(
  spec,
  coef,
  hyper,
  design,
  method,
  expected = TRUE,
  approx = "opg",
  pinned = NULL
)

Arguments

spec

A StatmodSpec().

coef

The coefficients.

hyper

The hyperparameters.

design

The design.

method

The outer method that estimated them, or NULL.

expected

Whether the information \(H\) is the expected one. The argument is not read where the model carries a filter, whose information is observed. The caller passes the information that the fit used, so that \(V_\beta\), \(H\) and the criterion's Hessian read one information.

approx

The approximation for the expected information. The argument is not read where the model carries a filter.

pinned

The coordinates that the fit left out of the criterion's determinant, as it records them in methods$pinned.

Value

A list with total, the scalar correction, per, one entry for each parameter and term, and n_hyper, the number of hyperparameters that were estimated. per uses only the diagonal of \(V_\theta\), so its sum differs from total when the estimated hyperparameters are correlated. The total and n_hyper are zero and per is empty where no hyperparameter was estimated. A zero total beside a positive n_hyper means that the curvature could not be read.

Details

The ordinary effective degrees of freedom treat the smoothing parameters as known, although they were chosen from the same data. Propagating their uncertainty into the coefficients gives the corrected Bayesian covariance

$$V' = V_\beta + J V_\theta J^\top, \qquad J = \partial\hat\beta/\partial\theta,$$

and the corrected count is \(\mathrm{tr}(V' H)\). \(J\) comes from the implicit function theorem at the penalized mode: differentiating \(\partial(-\ell + \rho)/\partial\beta = 0\) in the hyperparameter gives \((H+S)J_k = -\partial^2\rho/\partial\beta\,\partial\theta_k\), whose right-hand side is penalties7's penalty_cross(). \(V_\theta\) is the inverse of the negative of the outer criterion's Hessian, which statmod_marginal_hess() returns; the negative is taken because the criterion is maximized. The Hessian is that of the criterion that the fit maximized, so for ml() the determinant spans the range space of the penalty (integrated_basis()).

Everything is on the hyperparameter's link scale, which is the scale on which the outer criterion is optimized and therefore the only scale on which its Hessian is a variance.

The correction corresponds to the term of the effective degrees of freedom edf2 of mgcv that arises from the uncertainty of the smoothing parameters (Wood, Pya and Safken, 2016). The scale of a Gaussian response is a distribution parameter with its own coefficients here, so its uncertainty is part of \(H\) and needs no separate term.

The function returns zero, and n_hyper is zero, for every outer criterion other than reml() and ml(), including aic() and bic() used for a smooth penalty. A kinked penalty has no hyperparameter that the outer criterion estimates, because outer_hyper_index() skips it, so there is nothing to propagate and the correction is zero. The map from the hyperparameter to the penalized mode turns a corner whenever a coefficient joins or leaves the active set, and a delta method needs a derivative that does not exist there.

Where the criterion also estimates coefficients (marginal_coords()), the function returns marginal_edf_correction().

The mode of a model that carries a filter moves in the joint vector of the coefficients and the own parameters of the structural term, which is the vector that the determinant of the criterion spans. A penalty over those parameters is not a column of any design, so hyper_mode_cross() omits it when it is called for the coefficients alone. The correction is therefore computed on the joint vector. statmod_edf() takes the effective degrees of freedom of a structural model from joint_smoother_diag(), which reads the same two matrices, so the base count and the correction are both computed on the joint vector. The two matrices are those that statmod_marginal_full() and statmod_full_information() build, so that this function and the criterion use one assembly. The joint route reads the observed information, and expected and approx do not reach it. A model with no structural term of the filter shape takes the coefficient route, because statmod_marginal_full() returns NULL there.

References

Wood, S. N., Pya, N. and Safken, B. (2016). Smoothing parameter and model selection for general smooth models. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 111(516), 1548–1563.

See also
